newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh economy seen growing 5.4 pct in '96/97 - ADB.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh economy seen growing 5.4 pct in '96/97 - ADB.

text.p: Bangladesh's economy could grow 5.4 percent in the 1996/97 financial year provided fiscal and monetary reforms occur and private investment and savings are raised, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) said on Thursday.
The Manila-based bank said in its annual report Bangladesh's gross domestic product (GDP) could grow 6.0 percent in fiscal 1997/1998 (July-June) .
The country's GDP expanded 4.7 percent in 1995/96.
"Growth performance remains dependent on the agriculture sector, which is forecast to expand by over two percent in 1997 and 1998," the report said.
The agriculture sector is forecast to grow 2.4 percent in 1997 and 2.2 percent in 1998, it said.
The bank said 1996 growth in foodgrain production followed two years of stagnation and reached 19 million tonnes. This was five percent higher than in the previous two years.
It said good weather, improved fertilizer supply and a sharp rise in the price of rice during the plantation season contributed to the rebound in rice production.

The report said Bangladesh's industrial growth rate was expected to rise by 7.0 percent in 1997 and 9.5 percent in 1998. after falling to 5.7 percent in 1996 from 8.4 percent in the previous year. Much of the growth will be driven by the private sector, it added.

"To facilitate private sector growth, the government needs to improve the efficiency and flexibility of labour and financial markets, and to establish an effective commercial legal system for enforcing contracts and protecting property rights," it said.
The report said Bangladesh's fiscal deficit had been projected to decline to 5.5 percent of GDP in 1998 from 6.2 percent in 1996. It did not give a forecast for 1997.
"This will require strict budgetary control, rationalisation and simplification of tax rates, and stronger enforcement of revenue collection," it said.
Inflation is projected to be 4.0 percent in 1997, unchanged from 1996, and 4.5 percent in 1998.

Bangladesh's external trade position has improved "considerably" in the recent years, it said, adding that merchandise exports doubled and imports expanded by more than 50 percent between 1991 and 1995.
The current account deficit declined to 0.6 percent of gross national product (GNP) in 1995 from 7.2 percent in 1990.
The bank said the current account deficit is forecast to be about 4.7 percent in 1997 and 5.2 percent in 1998 of GNP.

However, the report said political unrest in 1996 restricted growth of external trade with exports declining to 11.8 percent in the year from 37.1 percent in 1995 and imports down to 17.9 percent from 39.4 percent in the previous year.
Exports are expected to rise by 14.5 percent in 1997 and 16.6 percent in 1998.
The report said Bangladesh must implement its reform programmes to reduce poverty.
It said urban poverty was alarming, with 61 percent of the urban population living below the poverty line in late 1995.
The average monthly income of urban poor households was only US$57.
